summary: Discusses differences between IS-IS as used to route IP traffic in RFC 1195 and the way it is deployed today, to help implementers, testers and operators. A companion document, RFC 3719, covers the ISO 10589 side. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The IS-IS rulebook and real networks do not match perfectly. This lists the differences so builders can make things work together.

questions: what is the is-is overload bit
narrow vs wide metrics in is-is
what is the difference between rfc 1195 and real is-is
subtitle: Where real-world IS-IS routing for IP differs from what RFC 1195 says, written for implementers and operators.

tldr.problem: IS-IS as used to route IP in networks today behaves differently from the RFC 1195 description in several places, which trips up implementers, testers and operators.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the differences one by one: unused TLVs, the Overload Bit, moving from narrow to wide metrics, the ISH PDU, the Attached Bit, default routes, mixed-protocol networks and IP interface address checks, and says what implementations should do.
tldr.outcome: It changes no protocol but gives practical guidance, such as including the IP Interface Address TLV in hellos so that adjacencies form with every implementation.

today: RFC 3787 is an Informational RFC and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it. It documents practice as of May 2004 and changes nothing in RFC 1195.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
Interior gateway protocols such as IS-IS provide timely information about the best routes inside a routing domain. The original design in ISO 10589 proved durable, but some choices have been modified. This document describes differences between the protocol in RFC 1195 and what can be observed on the wire today. A companion document, RFC 3719, covers the differences between ISO 10589 and current practice.

The document uses the RFC 2119 key words. It is a service to people implementing, testing and deploying IS-IS for IP.
sections.eli5: Some of the old rules no longer match how people really do things. This note writes down where.

sections.title: Unused Features and the Overload Bit
sections.content:
Two features in RFC 1195 are not in current use. The Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information TLV (code 131) is not used and MUST be ignored if received. The authentication TLV (code 133) has been replaced by TLV 10 from RFC 3567 and is also not used and MUST be ignored.

The Overload Bit was defined in ISO 10589 for a router that cannot store all the LSPs it receives, telling others not to use it for transit. Its meaning has been stretched: a router that has just rebooted can set it until BGP has converged, as described in RFC 3277. An implementation SHOULD use the bit to signal that it is not ready to accept transit traffic. It SHOULD NOT set the bit in pseudonode LSPs, and the bit seen in pseudonode LSPs SHOULD be ignored.

A receiver SHOULD treat all IP reachability advertisements from an overloaded router as directly connected in its SPF computation, so the overloaded router should take care which routes it advertises.
sections.eli5: Some old buttons on the control panel do nothing now, so you ignore them. One button, "I am busy, do not send me through traffic", is now used for more things than it was built for.

sections.title: Migrating from Narrow to Wide Metrics
sections.content:
The original TLVs (TLV 2, and TLV 128 and 130) carry a 6-bit link metric, which proved too limited. The Extended IS-Neighbors TLV (TLV 22) defines a 24-bit metric, and the Extended IP Reachability TLV (TLV 135) a 32-bit metric, both from RFC 3784. If not all devices in the domain support wide metrics, narrow metrics MUST continue to be used.

The transition algorithm has these ordered steps:

  1. All routers advertise and use only narrow metrics.
  2. Each system is configured in turn to send wide metrics as well; the two metrics for a link or prefix SHOULD agree.
  3. When all systems advertise wide metrics, each considers wide metrics in SPF and sets MaxPathMetric to 0xFE000000.
  4. Each system is configured in turn to stop advertising narrow metrics.
  5. Link metrics may then be rescaled to use the larger range.

While both styles exist, the SPF algorithm uses the minimum available metric for each link, so that different implementations compute the same distances.
sections.eli5: It is like switching from a ruler that only counts to 63 to one that counts much higher. Everyone first learns to use both rulers, and only then does anyone throw the old one away.

sections.title: Hellos, the Attached Bit and Default Routes
sections.content:
RFC 1195 requires point-to-point links to exchange ISO 9542 Intermediate System Hello (ISH) PDUs before IS-IS Hellos (IIH). In an IP-only network the original need for the ISH is gone, yet some implementations still require an ISH to start an adjacency. So an IP-only implementation SHOULD issue an ISH, as described in section 8.2.3 of ISO 10589. It may send an IIH alone, but that may not interoperate with those implementations.

For the Attached Bit, some implementations set the attachedFlag on IP routers when there is a default route in the local routing table or some other state implying a connection to the rest of the network.

RFC 1195 permits default routes only at level 2, as external routes. Because default routes are useful for other routing protocols and for influencing the exit point from an area, an implementation MAY generate default routes in Level 1.
sections.eli5: Two neighbors used to say a formal hello before talking. Some still insist on it, so it is polite to say it.

sections.title: Mixed Networks and Adjacency Rules
sections.content:
RFC 1195 assumes a homogeneous set of protocols: OSI only, IP only or dual. IP-capable routers MUST generate a Protocol Supported TLV (code 129) listing IP. A router that omits the TLV may be assumed to be pure OSI. Behaviour in mixed networks that do not follow the guidelines is not well defined, and ITU-T requires SONET/SDH equipment not to form an adjacency unless a network layer protocol is shared. Implementors MAY include that feature for interoperability with SONET and SDH DCN networks.

RFC 1195 says adjacencies form without regard to IP interface addressing, but many implementations refuse adjacencies based on interface addresses. Some do not interoperate with a neighbor that lacks the IP Interface Address TLV (132), and some will not form adjacencies on broadcast interfaces unless a common IP subnet exists. In a mixed LAN, DIS election may fail, producing several DISs or none, and black holes can follow. To interoperate, an implementation MUST include an IP Interface Address TLV in its IIH PDUs, and administrators should give numbered links a common subnet.
sections.eli5: Some neighbors will only shake hands if you wear a name tag and live on the same street. Wear the tag and pick matching streets, and everyone gets along.
